title: Graph canonization versus graph isomorphism
formal: Do there exist a deterministic oracle Turing machine A and a constant \(c\ge 1\) such that A, given any finite simple undirected graph G, computes a canonical form \(F(G)\) in at most \(O((N+1)^{c})\) steps using the graph-isomorphism decision oracle, where N is the input encoding length and F satisfies the conventions below?
why: Distinguishes recognizing structural equivalence from efficiently choosing a unique representative of each equivalence class.

progress.text: Babai gives a quasipolynomial canonical-form algorithm; the introduction leaves the general converse from efficient isomorphism testing unknown.
ICALP work gives canonical labelling guarantees for random regular graphs, without a general polynomial reduction to the decision oracle.

review_note: Specified a deterministic polynomial-time Turing reduction, binary graph encodings, unit-cost decision answers and canonical output as any consistent isomorphic representative. Did not impose a particular lexicographic form or replace canonization by pairwise isomorphism search.

references.locator: Discovery source; retrieved 2026-09-11. Evidence locator: polynomial-time equivalent

definitions: A graph G on \(n\ge 0\) vertices is given by n and the symmetric zero-diagonal binary adjacency matrix on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). Two such graphs G,H are isomorphic, written \(G\cong H\), if a bijection between their vertex sets preserves both adjacency and nonadjacency. The oracle takes two graphs in this encoding and returns YES exactly when they are isomorphic. Each oracle answer costs one step; writing the query and all other computation count toward the polynomial bound, so query lengths and number of calls are polynomial in N. Adaptive queries are allowed. The output \(F(G)\) is an adjacency matrix of a graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), with \(F(G)\cong G\). For every pair of input graphs, \(G\cong H\) must imply \(F(G)=F(H)\) as labeled matrices; the reverse implication then follows automatically. Thus one algorithm chooses a single representative for every isomorphism class. No particular representative, lexicographic minimum or vertex permutation is prescribed. The same deterministic machine and polynomial bound apply to all graphs; it has no other oracle or nonuniform advice. The empty graph has the empty matrix as its canonical form.
answer_criterion: A positive answer gives such an oracle algorithm and proves its worst-case polynomial running time, isomorphism preservation and identical outputs on every isomorphic pair. A negative answer rules out every deterministic polynomial-time algorithm with this decision oracle that computes any canonical-form function satisfying these conditions. A reduction that only finds an isomorphism between two supplied graphs does not suffice.

context_blocks.title: Recognizing a shape versus naming it consistently
context_blocks.text: Isomorphism asks whether two presentations describe the same graph after renaming vertices. Canonization takes just one presentation and returns a fixed presentation of that graph’s shape. For example, every relabeling of a three-vertex path must produce exactly the same three-by-three output matrix. It is insufficient to return a different isomorphic matrix depending on the input names. This consistency makes canonical forms useful for indexing and comparing stored structures.

context_blocks.title: The decision oracle gives only a bit
context_blocks.text: The oracle can compare any two explicitly constructed graphs, but returns only YES or NO. The question grants this ability at unit cost and asks whether polynomially much additional work can select consistent representatives. Finding a vertex matching for one given isomorphic pair has a different output requirement: its choices need not agree across every possible presentation of the same graph.

context_blocks.title: Known algorithms do not settle the reduction
context_blocks.text: Babai’s 2019 result gives general graph canonization in quasipolynomial time, meaning \(\exp (O((\log  n)^{d}))\) for a fixed constant d. It adapts the structure of an isomorphism algorithm and includes additional work to make choices canonical. Having quasipolynomial algorithms for both tasks does not establish a polynomial-time reduction that uses only decision answers.

context_blocks.title: Recent special cases
context_blocks.text: The ICALP 2026 paper obtains efficient canonical labelling for random regular graphs with high probability and recalls general quasipolynomial bounds. A guarantee for almost all graphs in a random model leaves exceptional and arbitrary input graphs uncovered. The present target is a deterministic worst-case reduction for every finite graph, and remains separate from the unrestricted question whether graph isomorphism itself lies in polynomial time.

sentences: Graph isomorphism recognizes when two labeled graphs have the same structure.
Canonization assigns every presentation of that structure an identical representative.
The question asks whether a polynomial-time algorithm can compute such representatives using only a graph-isomorphism decision oracle.
General quasipolynomial canonization and efficient results for random graph families do not supply this reduction.
A solution must handle every finite graph and keep its choices consistent across all relabelings.
